Despite significant advancements in the prevention of perinatal group B streptococcal (GBS) disease since the 1990s, GBS remains the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis in the United States. 2. In 1996, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in collaboration with relevant professional societies, published guidelines for the prevention of perinatal GBS disease. 3. During the 1970s, group B Streptococcus (GBS) emerged as the primary infectious cause of early neonatal morbidity and mortality in the United States. 4. Initial case series reported case-fatality rates as high as 50%. 5. Experts in GBS epidemiology, clinical microbiology, and pharmacology contributed to the development of prevention strategies. 6. The working group held regular teleconferences to identify potential areas for updating recommendations to prevent GBS disease and to define sources of newly available data, both published and unpublished, to inform guideline revisions. 7. A subset of topics was identified for in-depth review, including areas where new technologies or evidence had emerged since the publication of the 2002 guidelines, areas where implementation of the 2002 guidelines was suboptimal, and areas where interpretation of the guidelines was variable based on inquiries received by the CDC and expert experiences. 8. For these topics, a thorough review of published literature was conducted using PubMed searches, other sources (including abstracts and conference proceedings), and unpublished data from ongoing surveillance and research activities. 9. For topics with multiple data sources, evidence was summarized in tables. For topics with limited new evidence, summaries of relevant data were provided to working group members. 10. Expert opinions were sought from working group members on topics where no new evidence was available. 11. In June 2009, an in-person meeting of the technical working group was held to review available data and develop updated recommendations using an evidence-based approach when possible, and relying on expert scientific opinion when sufficient data were lacking. 12. These updated guidelines replace the CDC's 2002 guidelines and are intended for providers of prenatal, obstetric, and neonatal care, as well as supporting microbiology laboratories, hospital administrators, managed-care organizations, childbirth educators, public health authorities, and expectant parents and their advocates. 13. Evidence from at least one well-executed randomized controlled trial or one rigorously designed laboratory-based experimental study replicated by an independent investigator supports the recommendations. 14. GBS is a gram-positive bacterium that causes invasive disease primarily in infants, pregnant or postpartum women, and older adults, with the highest incidence among young infants. 15. Infections in newborns occurring within the first week of life are classified as early-onset disease, while late-onset infections occur in infants older than one week, with most cases evident during the first three months of life. 16. Due to the burden of disease among infants and the availability of effective interventions to prevent early-onset GBS disease, these guidelines focus solely on early-onset disease. 17. 18. GBS is the leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality among infants in the United States. 19. Prevention efforts have dramatically reduced the incidence of GBS over the past 15 years, from 1.7 cases per 1,000 live births in the early 1990s to 0.34–0.37 cases per 1,000 live births in recent years. 20. Based on data from the CDC's Active Bacterial Core surveillance (ABCs) system, GBS causes approximately 1,200 cases of early-onset invasive disease per year, with about 70% of cases occurring among term infants (≥37 weeks' gestation). 21. Infants with early-onset GBS disease typically present with respiratory distress, apnea, or other signs of sepsis within the first 24–48 hours of life. 22. The most common clinical syndromes of early-onset disease are sepsis and pneumonia; less frequently, early-onset infections can lead to meningitis. 23. The case-fatality rate of early-onset disease has declined from as high as 50% in the 1970s to 4%–6% in recent years, primarily due to advances in neonatal care. 24. Mortality is higher among preterm infants, with case-fatality rates of approximately 20% and as high as 30% among those ≤33 weeks' gestation, compared with 2%–3% among full-term infants. 25. 26. Neonatal infection primarily occurs when GBS ascends from the vagina to the amniotic fluid after the onset of labor or rupture of membranes, although GBS can also invade through intact membranes. 27. GBS can be aspirated into the fetal lungs, leading to bacteremia. 28. Infants can also become infected with GBS during passage through the birth canal; exposed infants may become colonized at mucous membrane sites in the gastrointestinal or respiratory tracts, but most colonized infants remain healthy. 29. Maternal intrapartum GBS colonization is the primary risk factor for early-onset disease in infants. 30. A classic prospective cohort study conducted during the 1980s revealed that pregnant women with GBS colonization were >25 times more likely than those with negative prenatal cultures to deliver infants with early-onset GBS disease. 31. In the absence of any intervention, an estimated 1%–2% of infants born to colonized mothers develop early-onset GBS infections. 32. Approximately 10%–30% of pregnant women are colonized with GBS in the vagina or rectum. 33. GBS colonization during pregnancy can be transient, intermittent, or persistent. 34. Although some women with GBS colonization during one pregnancy will be colonized during subsequent pregnancies, a substantial proportion will not. 35. The gastrointestinal tract serves as the primary reservoir for GBS and is the likely source of vaginal colonization. 36. Heavy colonization, defined as culture of GBS from direct plating rather than selective broth only, is associated with a higher risk for early-onset disease. 37. GBS identified in clean-catch urine specimens during any trimester is considered a surrogate for heavy maternal colonization and is also associated with a higher risk for early-onset GBS disease. 38. In addition to maternal colonization with GBS, other factors that increase the risk for early-onset disease include gestational age <37 weeks, prolonged rupture of membranes (≥18 hours), and intrapartum temperature >99.5°F (>37.5°C).
